steps.label: The RBF network
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Made from the lecture lec05-kp16 with view-from-text-v3: pages were planned first and each page is mainly one native infographic (designed in HTML and converted to native nodes), with the terms defined on the same page. 7 main pages plus 2 extension pages (not timed); sections 3 and 4 of the lecture are merged into page 3, and the extension exercises and worked answers share one page.

steps.label: Gaussian node
steps.speakerNotes: This is the first page of KP16. Prerequisites: generalized linear classifiers (KP13), which first change x into new coordinates with fixed functions and then learn a classifier linear in the weights; distance and norm, for example x equal to 0.5, 0.5 and c equal to 0, 0 give a squared distance of 0.25 plus 0.25, which is 0.5; and least squares (KP13). The product terms of KP15 react over the whole space, and this lesson asks whether we can use new coordinates that react only to nearby data. The answer is the radial basis function, a function of the distance to a centre c i, most often Gaussian. The RBF network g of x equals w0 plus the sum over i from 1 to k of w i times exp of minus the squared norm of x minus c i over 2 sigma i squared: one layer of Gaussian hidden nodes plus a linear output. In the upper plot a sigmoid node is high on a whole side of the line, a global response; in the lower plot three Gaussians each respond only near their own centre and fall to 0 away from it, a local response. It is close to a Parzen estimate, but Parzen has one kernel per training point, k equal to N, while here k is much smaller than N. Next, the next page covers local versus global response.

steps.label: Local versus global
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the Gaussian node. The previous page showed a Gaussian node reacting only near its own centre; this page asks what local versus global looks like in the plane. A global response runs along a whole hyperplane: the iso-set of a sigmoid node is a hyperplane, a family of parallel lines in two dimensions. A local response means the node answers only near its centre and goes to 0 away from it: the iso-set of an RBF node is a hypersphere, concentric circles around the centre in two dimensions. In the example on the right 2 sigma squared is 1, and at distances d equal to 0, 1, 2, 3 from the centre the Gaussian response e to the minus d squared is 1, 0.368, 0.0183, 0.000123; three units away the response is only one in ten thousand (program computed). Next, the next page covers XOR with two centres.

steps.label: XOR with two centres
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on local versus global response. The previous page showed that the iso-lines of an RBF are concentric circles. This page asks, with XOR, whether two such nodes are enough. Setup: k equal to 2, c1 equal to 1, 1, c2 equal to 0, 0, and y i equal to exp of minus the squared distance to c i, that is 2 sigma squared equal to 1. Point by point: the point 0, 0 has squared distance 2 to c1 and 0 to c2, so y is 0.135 and 1 and g equal to y1 plus y2 minus 1 is plus 0.135; 1, 1 is the same, also plus 0.135; the points 1, 0 and 0, 1 have squared distance 1 to both centres, so y is 0.368 and 0.368 and g is minus 0.264. The points 1, 0 and 0, 1 are mapped to the same point, that is folded together, and the single line y1 plus y2 equal to 1 separates the two classes. Back in the original space, g of x equal to 0 is a closed curve around the two centres, with 0, 0 and 1, 1 inside and 1, 0 and 0, 1 outside; far from every centre both exponentials go to 0 so g goes to minus 1, and far points all fall in the outside class, a feature of local response. Next, the next page covers fixed centres.

steps.label: Fixed centres
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on XOR with two centres. On the previous page the two XOR centres were chosen by hand and already enclosed a closed curve. With many data points, where do the centres come from? The simplest answer is fixed centres: pick k training points at random as the centres; with the centres fixed only w is left to learn, which is the linear problem of KP13, solved by least squares. The setup is my own design and reproducible: concentric-ring data with uniform angles, radius N(1.0, 0.15 squared) for class A and N(2.2, 0.2 squared) for class B, 100 points per class and 200 training points in total with random generator default_rng(0); new points 500 per class, 1000 in total, with default_rng(1); 2 sigma squared equal to 1; the prediction is the sign of g; for each k the centres are drawn once per seed 0 to 19, 20 times in all, and the new-point accuracy is averaged. For k equal to 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 the new-point accuracy is 56.0, 64.2, 76.1, 91.5, 99.5, 99.9 percent. More centres enclose the inner ring better; k equal to 16 is already almost all correct. Next, the next page covers choosing centres by clustering.

steps.label: Choosing centres by clustering
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on fixed centres. On the previous page random centres reached 99.5% on the ring data at k equal to 16, but every draw differs. This page asks whether clustering first and taking the group means always beats random. The clustering here is k-means: first split the data into k groups and use each group mean as a centre, then learn w by supervised least squares, a mix of unsupervised and supervised learning. The setup is my own design and reproducible: two moons, class A on the upper half circle cos t, sin t and class B on the shifted lower half circle 1 minus cos t, 0.5 minus sin t, with t uniform on 0 to pi and Gaussian noise of standard deviation 0.2; 60 points per class and 120 training points in total with seed 0; 500 new points per class, 1000 in total, with seed 1; 2 sigma squared equal to 0.6; k-means runs 50 rounds from randomly chosen initial centres; each k is run once per seed 0 to 19 and averaged. Random against k-means: k equal to 2 gives 76.3 against 73.5, 4 gives 84.4 against 83.1, 6 gives 90.5 against 92.7, 8 gives 93.3 against 95.0, 12 gives 94.9 against 95.2. The common myth is that clustering always beats random: at k equal to 2 and 4 random is slightly higher; from k equal to 6 clustering is higher, but the main difference is that it is steadier, with standard deviation 0.004 against 0.018 at k equal to 8. Next, the next page covers the price of locality.

steps.label: The price of locality
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on clustering. On the previous page the centres, whether picked at random or by clustering, had to fill the space where the data live. This page asks what happens as the dimension grows. The curse of dimensionality: as the dimension grows, the number of points or centres needed to fill the space grows exponentially, while data and centres are never enough. The setup is my own design and reproducible: 100 centres are placed uniformly at random in the unit cube 0 to 1 to the power l, and 2000 test points are drawn; random generator default_rng(0), used in sequence for l equal to 1, 2, 5, 10, 20; Gaussian width sigma equal to 0.3 and the response exp of minus d squared over 2 sigma squared, with d the distance from the test point to the nearest centre. Median distance to the nearest centre for l equal to 2, 5, 10, 20: 0.05, 0.30, 0.67, 1.22; the share of test points with response above 0.1 is 100%, 100%, 40%, 0%. For comparison a grid with 5 centres per axis needs 25, 3125 and 9,765,625 centres for l equal to 2, 5, 10. Next, the next page covers MLP versus RBF.

steps.label: MLP versus RBF
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the price of locality. The previous page showed that the price of locality is dimension: at l equal to 10 the 100 centres cover only 40% of the points. This page puts the MLP and the RBF side by side: the argument of a node is a weighted sum for the MLP and the distance to a centre for the RBF; the iso-set is a hyperplane for the MLP and a hypersphere for the RBF; the response is global for the MLP and local for the RBF; learning is slower for the MLP and faster for the RBF; generalization where training data are sparse is better for the MLP and worse for the RBF; and the number of nodes needed for the same performance is smaller for the MLP and much larger for the RBF. The table follows the source. To remember: an MLP thinks about which side of a hyperplane, an RBF about how near a centre; local learns fast but eats dimensions. Next, the next page covers ways to choose centres (extension).

steps.label: Ways to choose centres
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on MLP versus RBF. The previous page compared the MLP and the RBF: the RBF learns fast locally but needs many centres. This page is an extension, and the source lists six ways to choose centres: fixed centres, picked at random from the training points; trained centres, with w, c and sigma all by gradient descent, which is costly; clustering, k-means, with group means as centres; orthogonal least squares, which starts from many candidates and picks a compact set by forward regression, also estimating k; support vectors, which view the RBF network as a kernel map so that training is a quadratic programme with a global optimum and the number of centres is chosen automatically; and growing, where a new sample far from all centres with a large error becomes a new centre. Next, the next page covers the exercises (extension).

steps.label: Exercises
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on ways to choose centres. The previous page listed six ways to choose centres, and the XOR example used two centres chosen by hand. This page uses them for exercises: c1 equal to 1, 1, c2 equal to 0, 0, y i equal to exp of minus the squared distance to c i, g equal to y1 plus y2 minus 1, and g above 0 means omega 1. Q1: map 0.5, 0.5 to y and classify it; the squared distance to both centres is 0.5, y equals 0.607 and 0.607, g equals 0.607 plus 0.607 minus 1, which is plus 0.213, above 0, so class omega 1. Q2: for the far point 3, 3 the squared distances to c1 and c2 are 8 and 18, y equals 0.0003 and 1.5 times 10 to the minus 8, g is about minus 1.0, below 0, so class omega 2. Check: the middle point lies between the two centres and is enclosed by the curve; the far point falls to the bias minus 1 and takes the default class. That ends this unit; next, move on to the next unit.
